lessons.title: Drawing Out the Blade from Bar Stock
lessons.body: Start with a piece of high-carbon steel bar stock, like 5160 spring steel or 1084, about 25mm wide and 6mm thick. Cut a length of 150mm using a hacksaw or angle grinder. This will become your blade. Heat the steel in your forge until it's a bright orange-yellow, around 1100-1200Â°C. If you don't have a forge, build a simple one with a hole in the ground, charcoal, and a hairdryer for air. Once hot, place the steel on your anvil and strike it with a 2-3kg hammer. You want to draw out the steelâmake it longer and thinner. Work from the center outward, using the flat face of the hammer. Strike evenly on both sides to keep the blade straight. If the steel cools below a dull red, reheat it. Don't hammer cold steel; it will crack. For a camp knife, draw the blade out to about 200mm long and 3mm thick at the spine. Use the horn of the anvil or a hardy tool to help stretch the steel. Remember to keep the width consistent; you can use a pair of calipers to check thickness. This step takes timeâexpect to reheat the steel 5-10 times. Take breaks to avoid fatigue. In Africa, many smiths use old car leaf springs as source steel; they are tough and hold an edge well. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. Work in a well-ventilated area.

lessons.title: Forging the Bevels and Edge
lessons.body: Now that the blade is drawn out, it's time to form the bevels. The bevel is the sloping part that leads to the cutting edge. Heat the blade to a bright orange again. Place it on the anvil with the edge facing up. Using a hammer with a slightly rounded face, strike at about a 10-15 degree angle to create the bevel. Start with light blows to establish the bevel line, then increase force. Work from the base of the blade (near the handle) towards the tip. Flip the blade and do the same on the other side. You want the bevels to meet in the middle, creating a thin edge. Check your progress by looking at the blade from the edge; you should see a symmetrical triangle. If the edge gets too thin, it might fold over (called a cold shut). If that happens, grind it out later. For a camp knife, aim for a bevel height of about 15-20mm. Use a cross-peen hammer for faster material movement if you have one. Keep the blade hot; if it turns red, reheat. After forging the bevels, the edge might be wavy. That's normal; you'll straighten it later. This step requires practice to get even bevels. Take your time and don't rush. In many African workshops, smiths use a simple hammer and anvil to produce beautiful knives. Remember to anneal the blade if it becomes too hard to work; heat it to non-magnetic and let it cool slowly in ash or vermiculite.

lessons.title: Creating the Tang and Shoulders
lessons.body: The tang is the part of the blade that extends into the handle. The shoulders are the transition between the blade and the tang. To create the tang, you need to draw out a section of the steel at the base of the blade. Heat the base of the blade to orange. Using a hammer, strike the steel to reduce its thickness and width, but keep it long enough to go through your handle material. For a camp knife, the tang should be about 100mm long and 15mm wide, tapering slightly towards the end. You can use a hot cut or chisel to define the shoulders. The shoulders should be square and even; they will sit against the handle material. Work on both sides to keep the tang centered. If you have a guillotine tool or a spring fuller, use it to neck down the steel. Otherwise, use the edge of your anvil. Once the tang is formed, check that the blade and tang are in line. If not, heat and adjust. The tang should be thick enough to be strong but not too thick to make the handle heavy. Aim for about 4-5mm thick. After forging, let the blade cool slowly. You can now use a file to clean up the shoulders and tang. This step is crucial for a comfortable and durable handle. Many African blades have a stick tang, which is simple and effective. Practice on scrap steel first if you're new.

lessons.title: Straightening and Normalizing the Blade
lessons.body: After forging, the blade may be bent or warped. Straightening is done while the steel is hot. Heat the blade to a dull red (about 700-800Â°C) and place it on the anvil. Using a hammer, gently tap the high spots to straighten. You can also use a wooden mallet to avoid marring the steel. Check straightness by sighting down the blade or using a straightedge. Work quickly before the steel cools. Once straight, it's time to normalize. Normalizing relieves stresses and refines the grain. Heat the blade to non-magnetic (about 750-800Â°C) and then let it cool in still air. Do this three times. This cycle makes the steel softer and easier to file and grind. Don't quench it; just let it cool naturally. If you have a magnet, test: when the steel becomes non-magnetic, it's at the right temperature. After normalizing, the blade will have a uniform gray color. This step is often skipped by beginners, but it's important for a tough blade. In Africa, some smiths use a charcoal forge and judge temperature by color. Practice seeing the shades of red. Once normalized, the blade is ready for refining. Always handle hot steel with tongs and wear protective gear.

lessons.title: Refining the Profile with Files and Grinders
lessons.body: Now that the blade is normalized, you can refine its shape. Use a file to clean up the profile, remove hammer marks, and set the final edge. A 10-inch bastard file is good for this. Clamp the blade in a vise with the edge up. File from the ricasso (the flat area above the handle) towards the tip, maintaining the bevel angle. Use a file guide if you have one to keep angles consistent. For faster material removal, use an angle grinder with a flap disc or a belt grinder. But be careful not to overheat the steel; dip it in water frequently. You want a smooth transition from the bevel to the spine. The edge should be about 0.5-1mm thick before heat treating; any thinner and it might crack. Check symmetry by looking at the blade from the top. Use a sharpie to mark high spots and file them down. For the handle, shape the tang and shoulders so they are smooth. You can also drill holes in the tang for pins if you plan to use scales. In Africa, many smiths use simple files and stones to finish blades. Take your time; this step determines the final look and performance. After filing, the blade should be ready for heat treatment. Remember to clean the file often with a wire brush.

lessons.title: Practice Project: Forging a Simple Camp Knife
lessons.body: Now put it all together: forge a simple camp knife. Start with a 150mm piece of 5160 steel, 25mm wide and 6mm thick. Follow the steps: draw out the blade to 200mm, forge bevels, create a tang, straighten, normalize, and refine. For a camp knife, aim for a blade length of 150mm (6 inches) and a handle of 120mm. The spine should be about 3mm thick, with a full flat grind. After forging and refining, heat treat the blade. Heat to non-magnetic (about 800Â°C), quench in warm oil (canola or motor oil). Temper in an oven at 200Â°C for one hour, twice. This gives a hard edge and tough spine. Then finish with sandpaper up to 400 grit. Attach wooden scales using epoxy and brass pins. Shape the handle with a file and sand smooth. Sharpen on a stone. Test the knife by cutting rope and carving wood. If the edge chips, temper at a higher temperature (220Â°C). If it rolls, temper lower. This project teaches you the entire process. In Africa, you can sell such knives locally or use them for farming and camping. Practice makes perfect; make at least three knives to build skill. Always prioritize safety: wear gloves, glasses, and work in a ventilated area.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for forging high-carbon steel?
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel is forged at bright orange-yellow heat, around 1100-1200Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid hammering steel when it is cold?
options: A) It will bend too easily
B) It will crack or break
C) It will become too hard
quiz.explanation: Cold steel is brittle and can crack under hammer blows.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of drawing out the blade?
options: A) To make it shorter and thicker
B) To make it longer and thinner
quiz.explanation: Drawing out stretches the steel, making it longer and thinner.

quiz.q: Which hammer face is best for drawing out steel?
quiz.explanation: The flat face is used for general drawing out and flattening.

quiz.q: What is a cold shut?
options: A) A type of heat treatment
B) A fold in the steel from forging too cold
quiz.explanation: A cold shut occurs when the steel is folded over on itself at low temperature.

quiz.q: What angle should you hold the hammer to create bevels?
quiz.explanation: A slight angle of 10-15 degrees helps form the bevel slope.

quiz.q: How can you check if the bevels are even?
options: B) By looking from the edge
C) By measuring with a ruler
D) By tapping with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Looking from the edge shows if the bevels meet symmetrically.

quiz.q: What should you do if the blade becomes too hard to work during forging?
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens the steel by heating and slow cooling.

quiz.q: What is the tang of a knife?
options: B) The part that extends into the handle
C) The tip of the blade
quiz.explanation: The tang is the extension of the blade that goes into the handle.

quiz.q: What are the shoulders of a knife?
options: A) The transition between blade and tang
quiz.explanation: The shoulders are where the blade meets the tang.

quiz.q: What is a typical tang length for a camp knife?
quiz.explanation: A tang of about 100mm is common for a camp knife handle.

quiz.q: How thick should the tang be?
quiz.explanation: A tang of 4-5mm is strong yet not too heavy.

quiz.q: What tool can help define the shoulders?
options: A) A hot cut or chisel
quiz.explanation: A hot cut or chisel is used to cut in the shoulder lines.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep the tang centered?
options: B) For balance and handle fit
D) To make it easier to forge
quiz.explanation: A centered tang ensures the handle aligns properly and the knife balances.

quiz.q: What is normalizing?
options: B) Heating and slow cooling to relieve stress
quiz.explanation: Normalizing involves heating to non-magnetic and air cooling to refine grain.

quiz.q: How many normalizing cycles are typically done?
quiz.explanation: Three cycles are common to achieve good grain refinement.

quiz.q: At what temperature does steel become non-magnetic?
quiz.explanation: Steel loses magnetism around 750-800Â°C, indicating the right temperature for normalizing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of straightening the blade?
options: A) To make it look better
B) To ensure it is true and functional
quiz.explanation: A straight blade is essential for proper cutting and aesthetics.

quiz.q: When straightening, at what temperature should the steel be?
quiz.explanation: Dull red (about 700-800Â°C) is hot enough to move steel without damage.

quiz.q: What file is recommended for refining the blade profile?
quiz.explanation: A 10-inch bastard file removes material efficiently.

quiz.q: Why should you dip the blade in water while grinding?
options: A) To cool it and prevent overheating
quiz.explanation: Overheating can ruin the heat treatment, so cooling is necessary.

quiz.q: What is the ideal edge thickness before heat treating?
quiz.explanation: A thicker edge (0.5-1mm) prevents cracking during quenching.

quiz.q: What can you use to mark high spots on the blade?
quiz.explanation: A Sharpie marker is commonly used to mark areas to file.

quiz.q: What is a full flat grind?
options: A) A bevel that goes from edge to spine
quiz.explanation: A full flat grind has bevels that extend all the way to the spine.

quiz.q: What is the typical blade length for a camp knife?
quiz.explanation: A 150mm (6-inch) blade is common for camp knives.

quiz.q: What oil is commonly used for quenching?
quiz.explanation: Canola or motor oil are readily available and effective for quenching.

quiz.q: How many tempering cycles are recommended?
quiz.explanation: Two tempering cycles at 200Â°C for one hour each are typical.

quiz.q: What temperature is recommended for tempering a camp knife?
quiz.explanation: 200Â°C balances hardness and toughness for a camp knife.

quiz.q: What should you do if the edge chips during testing?
options: A) Temper at a higher temperature
B) Temper at a lower temperature
quiz.explanation: Chipping indicates the blade is too hard; tempering higher reduces hardness.

quiz.q: What is the final step in making a camp knife?
quiz.explanation: After heat treatment and finishing, the handle is attached.
